en: Freezing splits it. The protein and the water separate and no amount of shaking brings it back; use it in cooking if you have frozen some.

A cool, dark, airy spot — turmeric is a tropical rhizome and, like ginger, is chilling sensitive below about 12 °C (54 °F), so a few days out of the fridge does it no harm. It dehydrates and shrivels quickly in a dry kitchen.

Unpeeled, in a paper bag or a loosely closed box in the crisper. Cold is a compromise: the fridge is well below the 12–14 °C the rhizome actually wants, so expect skin darkening and pitting eventually, but it holds off mould and shrivelling for a couple of weeks. It stains everything it touches, cutting board and fingers included.
Freeze it whole and unpeeled, then grate from frozen — much the easiest way to handle it and no loss of colour.

Boiled udon is a 茹めん under Japan's 生めん類の衛生規範 and must be kept at 10 °C or below; the MHLW fresh-noodle HACCP guide requires it to be cooled to 10 °C promptly after boiling and held there. Go by the printed use-by date.
Sealed packs rely on an acid dip or post-pack pasteurisation. Once opened, cook within a day or two.
Udon freezes unusually well — commercial 冷凍うどん is sold this way. Boil from frozen; do not thaw first or it goes slack.
It is not safe to cook and eat a whole lobster if it is dead at the time of preparation.

Japan's MHLW HACCP guide for fried bean-curd products gives 厚揚げ (thick fried tofu) refrigerated storage at 10 °C or below and a use-by of roughly one week, and stresses that it must be chilled immediately after frying because the inside is still plain tofu.
Freeze in a bag with the air pressed out; the fried skin goes rancid before the tofu goes off.
Keep the bag at -18 °C or below, deep in the freezer rather than in the door, and do not overfill the cabinet — crowding blocks airflow and lets the temperature drift.

Do not thaw dumplings on the counter: the surface climbs into the 7-60 °C danger zone while the middle is still frozen, which the TFDA names as the biggest risk in home thawing. Boil or pan-fry straight from frozen, or thaw in the fridge and cook the same day. Never refreeze thawed raw dumplings.
Thawing in the refrigerator is not recommended.

TFDA’s festival advice is blunt: refrigerate or freeze, and never let them stand in the 7-60 °C range. Keep the bag at -18 °C or below and cook straight from frozen — thawed tangyuan collapse and the filling leaks out.

Only for a short wait before cooking. Cook the centre above 70 °C and keep boiling for 1-2 minutes after they float. Cooked tangyuan are a wet starch food — eat them hot and refrigerate leftovers below 5 °C for no more than a couple of days.

A dry starch flour with almost no fat, so it keeps well as long as it stays dry — humidity is the enemy, and a bag that has caked into lumps or smells musty has taken up water and should go. Keep it airtight, cool and away from the stove. Fermented cassava fufu flour has a sour smell when fresh; that is not spoilage.
The fine hairs rub off in handling; a bald, shiny melon is an older one. Keep it dry in the crisper.
Thicker-stemmed and hardier than most Asian greens. Bag it unwashed; trim and peel the woody stem base before cooking.
Taiwan's Ministry of Agriculture: rinse quickly, drain well, bag it and stand it stem-down in the bottom drawer of the fridge. The leaves wilt and go slimy fast once bruised.
Store unbroken bulbs in pantry.
Store individual cloves in refrigerator.
Wrap the bunch in slightly damp paper and bag it. Cut leaves smell strongly of garlic and will scent everything else in the fridge, so seal them properly.
MAFF's home vegetable freezing guide gives about 3 weeks: chop, dry off the surface water, bag flat and freeze.

Gazpacho is raw. Nothing in it has been cooked, so nothing has been killed — it is blended raw tomato, cucumber, pepper, garlic, oil, vinegar and bread, and it carries whatever the vegetables carried. AESAN's rule for cut fruit and vegetables is 4 °C or below; refrigerate gazpacho the moment it is made, in a covered jug, and keep it cold on the table in a jug standing in ice rather than out in the sun. Wash the vegetables properly before blending — that is the only control step this dish has.
Freezing splits it. The oil separates and the tomato goes watery and grainy; blending it again gets you most of the way back but never all of it. If you must, freeze it before the oil goes in.

Cool it fast and get it cold — this is the dish where that rule earns its keep. Uncooked rice carries Bacillus cereus spores that survive cooking, and Hong Kong's CFS is explicit that the toxins formed while those bacteria multiply cannot be eliminated by reheating: spread the rice out to cool from 60 °C to 20 °C within two hours and then to 4 °C within four, and keep the fridge at 4 °C or below. A covered pot of pilaf left on the stove overnight is the classic way to get ill. Reheat only once, and until it is steaming hot right through. If there is chicken or egg in the biryani, treat it as leftover meat and use it sooner rather than later.
Freeze it in meal-sized portions the day it is made, while it is fresh, and reheat from frozen.

As with kraut, room temperature is the fermentation, not the storage. NCHFP ferments dill pickles at 70–75 °F (21–24 °C) for about 3 to 4 weeks, and notes that regular dill pickles and sauerkraut are fermented and cured for about 3 weeks. Keep the cucumbers weighted under the brine and check the crock several times a week — Ohio State's instruction is to 'promptly remove surface scum or mold', because scum yeasts on the surface raise the pH and let softening organisms in.

NCHFP and Ohio State agree: fully fermented pickles may be stored in the original container for about 4 to 6 months, provided they are refrigerated and surface scum and moulds are removed regularly. They keep getting softer and more sour. NCHFP's advice for storing them longer is to can them — heat the brine to boiling, simmer 5 minutes, pack and process — which of course kills the culture.

Ohio State gives unopened canned foods 12 months. Cool, dark, dry, and out of the sun — light bleaches them and softens the texture long before anything else goes wrong. Vinegar-pickled gherkins are a high-acid food, so a sealed jar is genuinely stable; the failure modes are softening and colour loss, not safety, unless the seal has gone.

Ohio State gives opened canned pickles and olives 1 to 2 months refrigerated. Keep the gherkins below the surface of the vinegar and use a clean fork — a finger or a used fork is how the white surface film starts. Once they have gone soft and hollow they are past it, which usually happens well before two months if the jar has been in and out of a warm kitchen.

Store like any other dry rice: airtight, cool, dark and dry. Glutinous rice is higher in the amylopectin that makes it sticky and lower in amylose, but for storage purposes it behaves like white rice. Rice weevils get in through paper sacks — decant into a sealed container.
Once open, seal it. A musty smell means mould; do not wash it and use it anyway.
A cool larder or the fridge slows down both insects and the slow staling of the grain, which matters more in a humid summer.

Ohio State Extension's pantry chart gives ground spices and herbs 6 months and whole spices 1 to 2 years. Gochugaru is ground, so take the 6-month figure for full colour and aroma; it stays safe well beyond that but fades to a dull brown-orange. Airtight, opaque container, away from the cooker.

Korean households routinely keep 고춧가루 in the fridge or freezer, and in a humid climate that is the sensible choice — it holds the red colour, keeps the powder free-running and shuts out pantry moths. No agency publishes a cold-storage timeline for it, so no number is given here. Let a cold bag come to room temperature before opening it, or condensation will cake the powder.

Same reasoning as the fridge: freezing preserves colour and pungency indefinitely for practical purposes, but there is no published home figure. Double-bag it and portion it so you are not thawing the whole bag every time.
Unopened tubs keep to the printed date in a cool dark cupboard. Gochujang is a salty, sweet, fermented paste with low water activity — the salt and sugar are the preservation, not the cold.

Refrigerate once opened. Smooth the surface flat, lay the plastic disc or a piece of cling film straight onto the paste, and use a clean dry spoon. The colour darkens from bright red to brick over months — that is oxidation, not spoilage. Discard for fuzzy mould, an alcoholic or solvent smell, or bubbling that lifts the lid.

Gorgonzola dolce is a soft, wet, barely acidic cheese and should be treated as one: a fortnight at most at 0–5 °C, wrapped in waxed paper and then loosely boxed. The firmer, drier piccante will hold three to four weeks. Both keep ripening in the fridge — the blue veining spreads, the paste softens toward the rind, and the smell goes from sweet to ammoniac. Ammonia is the end point, not a phase.
Freezing wrecks the paste, which thaws crumbly and weeping. If you must, freeze it in cooking-sized lumps for sauces and accept that it will never go on a board again.

Ohio State's unopened hard-cheese figure, and a fair one for a waxed or vacuum-packed piece at 0–5 °C. Age matters more than anything else here: a jonge Gouda of four weeks is a moist, mild, semi-hard cheese that will not last like this, while an oude of a year or more is dry, salty and crystalline and effectively keeps itself.
Ohio State's opened hard-cheese figure. Waxed paper in a loose box; leave the red or yellow wax coating in place on the sides you have not cut, it is doing the job of a rind.
Fine for cooking cheese, grated. An aged Gouda is worth eating rather than freezing.
The hard orange shell protects the pulp; a lightly wrinkled shell means sweeter pulp, not spoilage.
In a bag so the shell does not dehydrate and crack.
Freeze the pulp with the seeds.
Freezing guidance applies to whole grapes.

Taiwan’s 農業部 advice for 仙草凍 and 愛玉 is to buy only what you will finish at one sitting, and if you must refrigerate it, not to keep it more than two days — sealed, lidded, and on the top shelf so drips from other food cannot land on it. These jellies are almost entirely water with no acid and no salt, so they have nothing to hold bacteria back.
Set jelly is not a pantry food. Unopened canned or retort grass jelly is, and follows its own printed date; once opened it becomes the fridge case above.
Freezing destroys it — the gel ruptures and drains into water on thawing.
Ripe is when this item is tender, fully developed and ready to eat. Note, these spoil quickly.
NMSU: 2 to 3 weeks at 45–50 °F (7–10 °C) and 90–95 % humidity, with chilling injury below that. Habaneros are small and thin-walled, so they shrivel before they rot — a wrinkled pod is still usable.
Freeze whole and unblanched, no headspace. Wear gloves when handling or chopping — capsaicin transfers to hands and then to eyes, and habanero is many times hotter than jalapeño.

A butcher's haggis, unwrapped and in its natural or synthetic casing, keeps like a fresh sausage — Ohio State gives fresh or smoked sausage 2 to 3 days at or below 4 °C. A vacuum-packed supermarket one keeps to its printed date instead. It is sold already cooked, but it is offal-based, moist and low-acid, so it must always be reheated right through before eating.

Reheated haggis and its leftovers are a cooked meat dish: 3 to 4 days at or below 4 °C, New Mexico State's figure. Cool it quickly and refrigerate within two hours; a whole hot haggis is a dense mass that holds warmth for a very long time, which is the real hazard with it.
Freezes well raw-packed or cooked. Thaw it fully in the refrigerator before reheating — a part-frozen centre in something this dense will not come up to temperature.
Unopened, in its sealed brine pack, up to the printed date — the high salt and the brine are what carry it, not the cheese itself.

Once cut, keep the block submerged in its own brine (top it up with a strong salt solution if you have poured it away) in a sealed tub at 4 °C or below. Halloumi is firmer and much saltier than a soft fresh cheese, but it is still a high-moisture cheese and Hong Kong's CFS notes Listeria grows at refrigerator temperatures as low as 0 °C — so if the brine turns cloudy or ropy, discard it.
Halloumi takes freezing better than most cheeses because it does not melt. Slice it before freezing and cook the slices from frozen.

Sealed, cool and dark. Halva is mostly sugar and sesame paste with almost no free water, which is why it sits on a shop counter unrefrigerated; what ends it is the sesame oil turning rancid, tasting sharp and bitter, not bacteria.

Wrap the cut face tightly against air. Oil beading on the surface and a crumbly, drier texture with age are normal. Keep it away from the stove and out of sunlight — heat is what accelerates the rancidity.

Worth it for a large slab or a warm kitchen, though the cold makes it hard and dulls the flavour; let it come back to room temperature before eating. Halva with fresh pistachio or chocolate through it keeps less well than plain.

Keep live in a shallow open bowl under a damp cloth at 4C or below. Purge in salted water at room temperature for no more than an hour, then get them straight back in the cold. Throw away any clam that stays open when tapped.
Freeze live in the shell in a single layer; cook from frozen without thawing.
Unopened tubes and tins, cool and dark, to the printed date.

Refrigerate once opened. In a jar, level the surface and pour a film of olive oil over it — that keeps the top from drying and darkening, and it is the traditional method. Clean dry spoon every time. A tube keeps better than a jar simply because no air gets back in.
Freezes well in teaspoon blobs on a tray, then bagged. No source gives a limit; several months is a fair ceiling.
Japan's MAFF: away from heat, sunlight and damp, tightly sealed.
Sealed. Rehydrated hijiki should be drained, refrigerated and used within a day or two; the soaking water is discarded.

Fresh horchata is a raw, unpasteurised, sweetened plant milk — ground tiger nuts or soaked rice, water and sugar, with nothing heated. That is a near-perfect growth medium, so keep it at or below 40 °F (4 °C) from the moment it is strained, in a closed bottle, and give it 2 to 3 days at most. It separates as it stands; shake it. If it fizzes, foams on pouring or tastes sharp, it has begun to ferment and it goes.

Freezing changes the texture — it thaws grainy and needs blending — but it works, and in Valencia frozen horchata is a drink in its own right, granizada, spooned half-frozen. Freeze it in a container with headspace.
Chill to 4C or below immediately and remove the gills and guts on the day of purchase.
Freeze as fillets, skin on and tightly wrapped - the dark flesh oxidises fast.
Fresh whole peppers will last longer if kept dry.
Peppers lose their crispness when frozen and thawed.
Will stay fresher longer if refrigerated.

Keep the galls whole and dry in a paper bag, not plastic — like any fungus they sweat and go slimy in a sealed bag. They darken from grey to black as they age, which is normal, but a sour smell is not.
Cook the galls down with onion and epazote first, cool, then freeze in portions. Raw huitlacoche freezes to mush.
Keep the pod closed until you eat it — the white pulp around the seeds browns within hours of being opened.
Whole pods only, in a bag. The pulp itself does not store.

Two different clocks run here. The safety clock: get the batter into the fridge at 4 °C or below as soon as it has risen, and do not leave it out to ferment for a second day in a warm kitchen — this is a starchy rice preparation, and Hong Kong's CFS notes that Bacillus cereus spores survive cooking and that the toxins formed while the bacteria multiply cannot be destroyed by reheating. The quality clock is much shorter: the culture keeps working in the cold, so batter that made light idlis on day one is noticeably sour by day three and by day five is only fit for dosas. Store it in a container half empty — it climbs. Never refreeze thawed batter.
Batter freezes in portions and thaws in the fridge overnight, but the culture takes a beating and the rise afterwards is weak. No source gives a limit; a month is a sensible ceiling.

Buy it labelled for raw eating (生食用), keep it at 4 °C or below, and use the printed date. The salt or soy cure is a seasoning, not a preservation step — MHLW states outright that salting, vinegar, soy sauce and wasabi do not kill Anisakis larvae.
Once opened, eat within about two days. Lift the eggs out with a clean dry spoon; a ready-to-eat raw food picks up whatever the spoon carries.

Freeze in small sealed portions and thaw slowly in the fridge — thawed fast, the eggs burst and go milky. MHLW's condition for killing Anisakis in raw seafood is −20 °C for 24 hours or more; the US standard it cites is −20 °C for 7 days or −35 °C for 15 hours.
Keep out of the sun; the skin wrinkles and the flesh goes mealy once it dehydrates.
Bag them loosely in the crisper. Taiwan's winter crop is sold crisp and eaten like an apple, and that crunch is the first thing to go.

Injera is a wet, spongy, live-fermented bread — much closer to a pancake than to a loaf. Keep the stack wrapped so it does not dry into a crisp, and eat it within a day or two; in a warm kitchen it grows surface mould quickly.
Wrapped airtight. It stiffens in the cold; steam it briefly or use it torn into firfir rather than as a fresh sheet.
Freeze the sheets interleaved with paper, flat, and thaw at room temperature.

Nissin sets 8 months from manufacture for packet noodles and 6 months for cup noodles. The limiting factor is the fried noodle block going rancid and the cup absorbing odours, so keep them out of sunlight and away from detergent, kerosene and strong spices — the polystyrene cup is porous to smells.
CTAHR: no more than 3 days at ambient temperature before decay sets in.
Chill as soon as possible after picking — CTAHR says field pre-chilling adds more than a week of life. Waxing plus a plastic wrap extends storage to 21 days at 53 °F (12 °C) commercially.
Freeze whole; the skins slip off easily after thawing for juice or jelly.
UH-CTAHR: fruit ripens in 3 to 7 days at 71–80 °F (22–27 °C). Keep it in a cool, well-ventilated place; fruit that fell from the tree lasts only 2 to 3 days.

CTAHR stores mature, undamaged whole fruit at 50 °F (10 °C) for 2 to 3 weeks. A 4 °C home fridge is colder than that, so expect nearer the short end and use cut flesh within 3 to 4 days in a sealed box.
Freeze the separated bulbs, not the whole fruit.

Airtight, cool, dry and dark — the enemy is humidity, not microbes. Jaggery keeps some of the cane's own molasses and moisture, so unlike white sugar it goes sticky, weeps a syrup, and grows a white bloom or fine mould in a damp kitchen; it also attracts ants and, in warm storage, sugar-loving beetles. Soft palm jaggery and nolen gur hold much more moisture than a hard cane block and belong in the fridge. A darkening block that has hardened is fine to use.
The right answer in a humid climate and for soft or liquid jaggery. Wrap it airtight — it takes up fridge odours and it sweats when you take it out.

NMSU: 2 to 3 weeks at 45–50 °F (7–10 °C) and 90–95 % humidity. Keep the pods dry and whole — a cut or bruised jalapeño rots from the wound. Colder than 45 °F brings chilling injury: softening, pitting and decay.

Wash, stem and pack with no headspace; jalapeños do not need blanching. NMSU gives up to 12 months in the freezer for properly packed chile. They thaw limp, so freeze them for cooking, not for slicing raw.

The same rule as serrano, and more so: ibérico is cured longer — commonly two to four years for a bellota leg — so it is drier and more stable still. Hang or stand it in a cool, dry, ventilated room out of the sun. The fat should look glossy and slightly oily at room temperature; that is the point of the breed and the acorns, and refrigeration ruins it. Cover the cut face with its own trimmed fat between sessions.

For sliced ibérico only. Once a vacuum pack is opened the slices dry and oxidise within days; re-wrap them tight and eat them soon. Never refrigerate the whole leg. Take sliced ibérico out 20 to 30 minutes before serving — cold ibérico fat is waxy and tastes of nothing.
Not recommended for anything you intend to eat as ham. The high oleic fat that makes ibérico worth the money is exactly what oxidises in a freezer.
Unopened vacuum packs keep refrigerated until the date on the pack. Lay them flat; a pack that has lost its vacuum and gone puffy goes back to the shop.

This is the number that matters. Once the vacuum is broken — or once a shop has sliced it for you over the counter — the ham is an opened ready-to-eat meat, and it dries, oxidises and browns fast. Re-wrap tightly in film with the slices touching, at or below 40 °F (4 °C), and eat within a few days. Let it come to room temperature on the plate, not in the packet.
Freezing sliced jamón is a compromise: the fat oxidises and the texture goes waxy. Freeze it interleaved with paper and use it in cooking rather than on a board.

A whole jamón is shelf-stable by design: the official IGP Jamón Serrano specification states that once the curing process is finished the ham may remain at room temperature. Hang it or stand it in a cool, dry, airy room, 15–20 °C, out of direct sun, and never in a sealed bag or the fridge. Once you cut into it, cover the exposed face with its own fat and a cloth and keep working across the same face; a started ham should be finished within a few weeks to a couple of months before the cut face dries out and turns rancid.

Do not refrigerate a whole leg. Cold hardens the fat, kills the aroma and brings condensation and surface mould when you take it out. A cool larder or the coolest room in the house is the right place.
Have the fishmonger kill and clean it; hold at 4C or below. Raw eel blood contains a heat-labile toxin, so eel is always cooked, never eaten raw.
A very oily fish - wrap in two layers and use well inside the quality window.
1-2 weeks if inappropriately handled.
Free from moisture; chilling injury causes decay, discoloration or loss of texture may occur.
NCHFP: most dried fruit keeps about 1 year at 60 °F (16 °C) and 6 months at 80 °F (27 °C). Airtight jar, dark cupboard, away from the stove.
Ohio State advises refrigerating dried fruit if possible; in a humid climate this also stops the dates going sticky and mouldy.
Double-bagged; freezing also kills any pantry moth eggs in a new packet.
Eaten green and crunchy or ripened to golden and soft; leave it out to move from one to the other.
Green fruit keeps longer than ripe; bag it so the skin does not shrivel.

Unopened, use the printed 賞味期限. Japan's food sanitation standards require 特殊包装かまぼこ to be stored at 10 °C or below unless the pack was heated to 120 °C for 4 minutes in a sealed container, or has pH 4.6 or lower, or water activity 0.94 or lower.
